clue.text: Outstanding work for a player to record

parts.note: a back is a player in a defensive position, as in rugby or football
to log something is to record it in writing

explanation.surface: Someone describes a musician's unfinished recording session as overdue work.
explanation.definitionFit: A backlog is an accumulation of tasks still waiting to be done.

clue.text: Eg Sir Thomas Bertram's circle in a Greater London suburb

indicators.note: the round letter sits inside the suburb's name

parts.note: Barnet is a borough and suburb in north London
a circle is shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A literary note placing a Jane Austen character's social set in an outer London district.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Thomas Bertram, of Austen's Mansfield Park, holds a hereditary title just below a peer; BARNET is a suburb of north London.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas Bertram is an example of a hereditary titled commoner, ranking below the peerage.

clue.text: Carmen's first song about entertainment in a restaurant

indicators.note: first takes just the opening letter of Carmen's
the song wraps around the word for entertainment

parts.note: an aria is a solo song in opera
a fete is an outdoor entertainment or fair

explanation.surface: An opera singer performs her first number at a party held in a dining place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' sets the entertainment word inside the song, so the song is split around it; 'Carmen' suggests the opera, a neat distraction.
explanation.definitionFit: A cafeteria is a self-service eating place, a kind of informal restaurant.

clue.text: The Spanish queen destined always to fall?

parts.note: los is a Spanish word for 'the' (masculine plural)
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A Spanish queen whose fate is to be toppled for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: someone always destined to fail or lose out.
explanation.definitionFit: A perennial failure is someone fated never to win, always going down.

clue.text: Bizarre quest, ergo misplaced

indicators.note: letters put in the wrong places are being rearranged

explanation.surface: A strange search, therefore one gone astray.
explanation.definitionFit: Grotesque means weirdly distorted, so strange as to be bizarre.

clue.text: Source of colouring permitted in savoury pie?

indicators.note: the word for permitted sits inside the savoury item

parts.note: pâté is a savoury paste, often baked in a crust, hence the question mark
to let means to permit or allow

explanation.surface: A cook wonders whether colourings are allowed in a meat pie.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter's palette holds the paints from which colours are mixed.

clue.text: Piling up fattening food, you initially get short-winded

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of each word from Piling to you

explanation.surface: A warning that heaping on rich food will leave you out of breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' looks as if it applies only to 'you', but it takes the first letter of all five words.
explanation.definitionFit: Puffy describes someone breathing hard, panting, out of breath.

clue.text: Russian city's loan covering grain production

indicators.note: the loan word wraps around the rearranged grain

parts.note: to lend is to make a loan

indicators.note: production signals the grain letters are worked into a new form

explanation.surface: A Russian city borrows money to cover its grain output.
explanation.walkthrough: 'production' rearranges the grain letters, and 'covering' puts the loan word around them; Leningrad was the Soviet name of St Petersburg.
explanation.definitionFit: Leningrad was the Soviet-era name of St Petersburg, a major city in Russia.

clue.text: He attempts to involve Republican in row

indicators.note: the row takes in the Republican letter

parts.note: a tier is a row of seats

explanation.surface: Someone trying to drag a Republican into a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' suggests a quarrel, but it is a row of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: A trier is a person who keeps making an effort to succeed.

clue.text: Soldiers put up notice round lake in this island

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up reads it from the bottom

parts.note: REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British army corps

indicators.note: the notice goes round the lake letter

parts.note: an ad is a notice or advertisement
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Troops post a sign near a lake on an isle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' reverses REME to EMER; 'this island' points to the Emerald Isle, Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Emerald Isle is a poetic name for Ireland, a green island.

clue.text: William caused a lot of commotion after the game

indicators.note: after puts the commotion word behind the game

parts.note: RU is Rugby Union

indicators.note: a lot of, not all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a fuss is a commotion

explanation.surface: Someone named William caused a scene after a match.
explanation.walkthrough: William II of England was nicknamed Rufus; 'caused' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: William Rufus was King William II, so Rufus names that William.

clue.text: Drive causing displeasure

explanation.surface: A campaign that upsets people.
explanation.definitionFit: A military drive or attack is an offensive; something giving offence is unpleasant and objectionable.

clue.text: Sort of tie no politician accepts — it brings disrepute

indicators.note: sort of suggests a variant form, so the tie no letters and the politician are rearranged together

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party, taken in with the tie no letters

explanation.surface: A Conservative MP wears a disreputable kind of tie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accepts' joins the politician to TIE NO, and 'Sort of' rearranges the combined letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Notoriety is fame for something bad, the disreputable kind of renown.

clue.text: Name given in Catechism by a Bellini heroine

parts.note: the Prayer Book Catechism asks 'What is your name?' with the answer printed N or M

explanation.surface: A name taken from the Catechism belongs to an opera heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Book of Common Prayer Catechism the reply to 'What is your name?' is printed 'N. or M.', leaving the name to be filled in.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma is the title role of Bellini's opera, a Druid priestess.

clue.text: Faulty delivery worth changing

indicators.note: changing signals that the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A poor ball bowled that is worth altering.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a ball thrown, with a straightened arm, instead of bowled is illegal.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a throw is an illegal bowling action, a no-ball.

clue.text: Occidental bird inhabiting a German river

indicators.note: the bird lives inside the river

parts.note: the Weser is a river in northern Germany
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A western bird living on a German river.
explanation.definitionFit: An occidental is a person from the West.

clue.text: Animal seen in court eating fruit

indicators.note: the court takes the fruit inside it

parts.note: a quad is a quadrangle, a courtyard
a drupe is a stone fruit such as a plum

explanation.surface: A creature spotted in a courtyard eating fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A four-footed animal is any creature walking on four legs.

clue.text: The writer could be Thoreau's son? Certainly not

indicators.note: could be suggests the letters may form something else

parts.note: the name with its possessive S counted as a letter

explanation.surface: Might this writer be Thoreau's child? No.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Certainly not' adds the joke: the writer is a woman, so no son.
explanation.definitionFit: Authoress is an old term for a female writer.

clue.text: By introducing close' relative, man upset the staff

parts.note: per means by, as in per annum
a son is a close relative

indicators.note: upset in a down clue turns the word over, reading it upwards

parts.note: Len is a man's name

explanation.surface: A man upsets the workforce by bringing in a relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses LEN to NEL. The stray apostrophe in close' is a print slip.
explanation.definitionFit: Personnel are the people employed by an organisation, its workforce.

clue.text: Temporary passage crossing, quarters

indicators.note: the passage goes across the quarters, enclosing them

parts.note: transit is passage from one place to another
E and N are compass quarters, east and north

explanation.surface: A temporary route crossing living quarters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something transient lasts only briefly, passing away soon.

clue.text: Cockney thief — a stranger, maybe

explanation.surface: A Londoner talks about a criminal who may be unknown.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang it rhymes with thief; folklore says a leaf floating in your cup foretells a stranger's visit.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang uses it for a robber; superstition reads a floating leaf in a cup as a visitor coming.

clue.text: Order given by woman, almost a hundred

indicators.note: almost means the last letter is missing

parts.note: Doris is a woman's name
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A command issued by a woman, almost a century old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' means a classical style of architecture, not a command.
explanation.definitionFit: Doric is one of the classical orders of architecture.

clue.text: Volatile substance used in temporary lodgings, or outside entrance to hostel

parts.note: a camp provides temporary lodging

indicators.note: the entrance to a word is its first letter

parts.note: or taken as written, standing outside, beyond the hostel letter

explanation.surface: A volatile chemical used in a camp, or outside the door of a hostel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' only places OR beyond the hostel letter; 'used in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Camphor is an aromatic compound that evaporates readily, used in mothballs.

clue.text: Consent to king being carried by a horse

indicators.note: the king sits inside the horse

parts.note: gee, or gee-gee, is a child's word for a horse
R is Rex, king

explanation.surface: A king agrees to ride a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: To agree is to give consent or assent.

clue.text: Not strict with soldiers at first — stand easy!

indicators.note: at first puts the soldiers ahead of the rest

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers
lax means not strict

explanation.surface: Drill-sergeant orders: be lenient with the troops at first, then at ease!
explanation.definitionFit: Stand easy is a military order to ease off, to unwind.

clue.text: Family with occasion to store goods here

parts.note: stock is lineage or family
room means occasion or scope, as in no room for doubt

explanation.surface: A family has a chance to keep their goods somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A stockroom is a storage area where merchandise is kept.

clue.text: Move quickly to make a dress

explanation.surface: Hurry to make a frock.
explanation.definitionFit: To shift is to go fast in British slang; a straight loose frock is also called this.

clue.text: Weekend cut out for a boat

parts.note: the end of week is its last letter, K
to etch is to cut a design out

explanation.surface: A weekend carved out for sailing.
explanation.definitionFit: A ketch is a two-masted sailing vessel.

clue.text: A bloomer, say money dropped in road

parts.note: eg means for example, which say also means

indicators.note: the money falls inside the road

parts.note: a lane is a narrow road
tin is slang for money

explanation.surface: Someone makes a mistake, dropping cash in the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomer' suggests a blunder, but here it is a flowering plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Eglantine is the sweet briar, a wild rose that flowers.

clue.text: Fish found in ditch, not river

indicators.note: not means the river letter is left out

parts.note: a trench is a ditch

explanation.surface: A fish turns up in a ditch rather than a river.
explanation.definitionFit: The tench is a freshwater fish of the carp family.

clue.text: Steps taken to identify character. Golf comes next

definitions.text: taken to identify character. Golf comes next

explanation.surface: Dance steps used to spell out a letter, with golf to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: In the NATO phonetic alphabet the word stands for the letter F, and Golf, for G, comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: This ballroom dance is a sequence of steps; in radio spelling it is the code word for F, followed by Golf.

clue.text: Savant's description of a star outside church

indicators.note: the star word goes around the church

parts.note: solar describes the Sun, a star

explanation.surface: A learned man's account of a star around a church.
explanation.definitionFit: A scholar is a learned person, as a savant is.
